_notes: The guided record is shown first with the clock paused; other records follow in game_data order. Words in curly braces are placeholders the game fills from the data.

1.title: Can I trust where this came from?
1.briefing: Check every seal before the numbers: an untrusted report is blocked, whatever it says. Limit: {flop_limit} training FLOPs per lab. You have {shift_time}.

L1-007.hint: The numbers look fine. Check the seal.

L1-003.hint: What does this add to the tally?

L1-005.hint: Check the owner's total, not the job.

L1-006.hint: Close to a line. Read the tally.

questions.prompt: L1-007 was under every limit. What gave it away?
questions.explanation: It was edited after signing. Forgeries can have normal numbers.

questions.prompt: L1-008's signature is valid for chip-99's own key. Why isn't that enough?
questions.model_answer: Anyone can make a key pair and sign anything. The registry is the manufacturer vouching that a key lives inside a real metering chip. Without that, the "meter" could be a script.
key_points: A valid signature only shows that the holder of that key signed it
Anyone can create a key pair
The registry (endorsement) is what ties a key to a genuine chip

questions.prompt: Which field can a lab change without breaking the seal?
questions.explanation: declared_type is a sticky note. Remember this for Level 3.

2.title: Have I seen this before, and who is really paying?
2.briefing: New period, totals reset. Labs now resend old reports and split big jobs. Watch counters and charge the registered owner. Energy limit: {energy_limit} kJ. You have {shift_time}.

guided_steps.text: Who pays? The registered owner, {owner}. The lab picks job and record IDs.

L2-003.hint: What's already on this owner's account?

L2-005.hint: Small alone. What else did this owner run?

L2-007.hint: Seen these numbers before? Check the counter.

questions.prompt: L2-007 and L2-008 are identical, with valid seals. What shows L2-007 is a replay?

options.b: Counter 1 isn't above chip-12's last accepted, 1

questions.explanation: Record IDs are sticky notes. The sealed counter shows it isn't new.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a valid signature stop a replay?
questions.model_answer: The seal proves who made the report and that it hasn't changed, not when it was made. An old genuine report is still genuine.
key_points: The signature proves origin and integrity
It says nothing about when the report was made
An old genuine report still verifies, so freshness needs its own check (the counter)

questions.prompt: Why charge the registered owner, not the job ID?
questions.model_answer: The lab chooses job IDs and can split one run across many; job_016 even appears under two labs. The owner comes from the registry, tied to a key the lab cannot change.
key_points: Job IDs are chosen by the lab
Splitting one run across job IDs would dodge the cap
The registered owner is bound to the chip's key by the registry

3.title: Is the claim true?
3.briefing: Labs label training runs as inference to dodge the FLOP cap. The label is theirs; the measurements aren't. You have {shift_time}.

questions.prompt: L3-002 passed every trust check. Why didn't its seal stop the false label?
questions.model_answer: declared_type sits outside the envelope. The chip never measured or signed it, and the sealed measurements contradict it.
key_points: declared_type is unsigned (a sticky note)
The seal only covers the measured fields
The FLOPs-per-kJ ratio contradicts the claim

questions.prompt: L3-004 seals the same FLOPs as lab_01's Level 2 report, but used 16× the energy. Both seals are valid. What happened, and what does it say about signatures?
questions.model_answer: The FLOP meter missed work that the energy meter saw. A seal proves the chip reported this number unchanged, not that the number is complete.
key_points: The FLOP meter undercounted work it can't see
The energy reading revealed the hidden work
A signature shows a number is authentic, not that it is complete or true

questions.prompt: L3-003's ratio (463 × 10⁹) fits both bands. What can you conclude?

options.b: The claim fits but isn't proven

questions.explanation: The bands overlap from 376 to 610 × 10⁹, where the gauge can't tell them apart.

4.title: How sure do I need to be?
4.briefing: Final shift. Meters are noisy, and every old trick is back. You have {shift_time}.

L4-001.hint: Overlay on. Check the energy bar.

L4-002.hint: Where does energy sit against the shading?

L4-004.hint: Which of this owner's reports were trusted?

L4-005.hint: This owner has been here before.

L4-006.hint: Compare energy with the cap itself.

questions.prompt: L4-001 read 4.49 kJ, under the 4.6 kJ cap. Why block it?

options.b: Readings can be 5% low, so it may be over
options.c: lab_23 is over the FLOP cap

questions.explanation: Above 4.37 kJ, noise means it could really be over 4.6.

questions.prompt: The energy margin and the profile tolerance lean opposite ways. Why?
questions.model_answer: The energy margin accepts some false blocks so a hard cap is never missed. The profile tolerance accepts some borderline jobs so honest runs, whose ratio naturally varies, aren't blocked (L4-010).
key_points: The energy margin is fail-closed: it blocks some honest jobs to avoid missing violations
The profile tolerance is fail-open: it allows borderline jobs to avoid blocking honest ones
Each trades false blocks against missed violations

questions.prompt: Under time pressure, which check would you automate first, and which would you keep a person on? Why?
questions.model_answer: Automate the registry, seal and counter checks: they are mechanical and exact. Keep a person on the workload-profile and borderline-noise calls, which need judgment.
key_points: The trust checks (registry, seal, counter) are mechanical, so automate them
The profile and noise calls involve judgment and uncertainty
The answer ties the choice to the speed-versus-care trade-off
